metrics.label: Net fees
metrics.method: I treat FY2026 as a late-downturn stabilisation year, not a recovery. The same-period annual base is FY2025 net fees of £972.4m. Applying an approximately 7.8% reported decline gives £972.4m × 0.922 = £896.5m, rounded to £897.0m. The exit-rate angle is less negative: Q4 reported fees were down 4% (5% LFL), with Temp & Contracting down 3% and Perm down 7%; this supports a result above an extrapolation of FY2025's 13% reported fall, but does not support a return to growth. The company’s mix evidence also supports partial stabilisation: Temp volumes were stable in Q4 and higher Perm fees (+3%) offset some volume pressure. Pulling the other way, Germany is 32% of group fees and its Engineering line was down 20%, while peer disclosures still show European/German weakness; country exits/disposals contributed about £15m of FY2026 reported fees, making reported comparability less clean. I weight the FY2025 annual base plus H2/Q4 run-rate most heavily, use the cycle history to reject a straight-line FY2025 decline, and make a modest allowance for positive Q4 FX versus LFL. This prioritises same-year annual seasonality and the company’s latest outturn over the UK-only improvement in July news.
assumptions: FY2026 reported group net fees decline about 7.8% from FY2025, after a materially better Q4 reported decline of 4%.
Temp & Contracting remains more resilient than Perm, broadly consistent with Q4 declines of 3% and 7%, respectively.
The approximately £15m FY2026 contribution from exited/disposed countries is included in reported net fees, while underlying continental-European demand remains weak.
FX is a modest support to the reported FY2026 comparison late in the year, consistent with Q4 reported growth being one percentage point better than LFL.
drivers_applied: Client/candidate confidence and weak Perm conversion
Germany contractor-hours, Engineering and automotive exposure

metrics.label: Pre-exceptional basic EPS
metrics.method: EPS is built from the guided profit outcome rather than from statutory Yahoo EPS, because the requested basis is pre-exceptional basic EPS. FY2025 pre-exceptional basic EPS was 1.31p on £45.6m pre-exceptional operating profit. Applying the forecast profit ratio gives 1.31p × (£46.0m/£45.6m) = 1.32p. I then add 0.10p for a modestly better conversion of operating profit into attributable earnings and a slightly lower effective share base than the FY2025 full-year base is likely to imply, yielding 1.42p. A second cross-check uses H1 FY2026 weighted-average shares of 1,595.7m: 1.42p implies approximately £22.7m pre-exceptional earnings, or 49.3% of £46.0m operating profit. That sits between FY2025's depressed implied conversion (about 46%) and FY2024's stronger implied conversion (about 61%), hence is deliberately not a recovery-level EPS assumption. Cost savings/productivity protect operating profit, but weak hiring volumes and finance/tax uncertainty limit the EPS uplift. This follows the required intuition where profit/EPS operational leverage can exceed fees but should not be extrapolated into a broad-cycle rebound.
assumptions: FY2026 pre-exceptional operating profit is £46.0m and exceptional restructuring/property charges are excluded from both forecast EPS and operating profit.
Weighted-average basic shares are approximately 1.596bn, close to the reported H1 FY2026 1,595.7m.
Pre-exceptional earnings conversion from operating profit is about 49%, modestly above FY2025's implied level but below FY2024's level.
No material tax, net-finance-cost, or buyback effect changes pre-exceptional basic EPS by more than roughly 0.15p versus this build.
drivers_applied: Structural cost savings and consultant productivity
Weak Perm conversion and lower fee base
Finance cost/tax and basic share-count sensitivity
Exclusion of restructuring and property-impairment exceptional items

metrics.label: Pre-exceptional operating profit
metrics.method: The primary angle is the exact-period latest company outlook: Hays expected FY2026 pre-exceptional operating profit at the top of the external £37.0m–£46.0m consensus range, which gives £46.0m directly. The historical-base angle is £45.6m in FY2025; £46.0m is therefore £0.4m, or 0.9%, higher despite lower forecast fees. That is credible because Q4 productivity rose 8% year-on-year and management said cost discipline offset lower H2 fees, with about £50m annualised savings achieved and lower consultant headcount. The margin cross-check is £46.0m / £897.0m = 5.13% conversion, versus FY2025's 45.6/972.4 = 4.69%, a 44bp improvement: material but far below the FY2023 cycle-high conversion of about 15%, and therefore consistent with a trough, not a recovery. The conflicting peer angle is adverse—Robert Walters and SThree show that cost action does not fully immunise recruiters from Europe/Germany volume weakness—so I do not forecast above the stated top-end indication. Q4 fee stabilisation and the company’s own near-complete-year visibility outweigh peer evidence for this reported period.
assumptions: Hays' statement that FY2026 profit will be at the top of the £37.0m–£46.0m consensus range means approximately £46.0m pre-exceptional operating profit, not an amount materially above it.
Approximately £50m annualised cost savings and reduced consultant headcount offset lower FY2026 net fees sufficiently to lift conversion by about 44bp year on year.
The expected approximately £40m restructuring charge and approximately £30m right-of-use property impairment are exceptional and excluded from this pre-exceptional forecast.
No late June accounting adjustment or FX movement causes the result to fall materially below the top-end outlook.
drivers_applied: Structural cost savings and lower headcount
Exclusion of exceptional restructuring and property charges

metrics.conflicts_resolved: The company outlook is not formal numerical guidance but is the latest first-party exact-period statement and takes precedence over extrapolation. It conflicts with weak European peer results only to the extent that peers suggest downside risk; I retain £46.0m rather than exceed it because Hays' own statement already incorporates its data through Q4. forecast.reconciliation: The filings report is decisive: it provides the FY2025 comparable bases, the 10 July FY2026 Q4 exit-rate/outlook, the pre-exceptional accounting basis, and quantified cost/productivity drivers. The news report is a currency check only: UK temp/placement stabilisation corroborates the Hays Q4 improvement, while Robert Walters/SThree prevent calling a broad European recovery. The financials report is a shape/unit check: it confirms that gross profit is Hays net fees and warns that its operating income and EPS are statutory, not the requested pre-exceptional measures. Accordingly, profit is anchored to Hays' top-of-range indication; fees are built from FY2025 plus the Q4 stabilising but still negative run-rate; EPS is derived from the profit forecast, prior pre-exceptional EPS, share count and conservative earnings conversion.
forecast.sanity_checks: Net fees: £897.0m is -7.8% year on year from £972.4m; this is plausible because FY2025's -13% decline moderates with Q4 reported fees only -4%, but Perm conversion, Germany and public sector remain weak. Net fees 897.0 is GBP millions, i.e. £0.897 billion, not £897,000m or statutory turnover. It is within the stated 300–1,800 GBPm band. Pre-exceptional basic EPS: 1.42p is +8.4% year on year from 1.31p; this is plausible because guided profit is marginally higher and productivity/cost action improve conversion despite lower fees. EPS 1.42 is 1.42 pence per basic share, not £1.42 and not 0.0142 pence. It is within the stated -10 to 30 GBp band. Pre-exceptional operating profit: £46.0m is +0.9% year on year from £45.6m; this is plausible because £50m annualised savings and productivity offset lower fees, and it precisely reflects the stated top of the £37m–£46m range. Operating profit 46.0 is GBP millions, i.e. £46.0 million, not £46.0 billion; exceptional charges are excluded. It is within the stated -100 to 400 GBPm band.
forecast.known_weaknesses: FY2026 audited results were not public at the 16 August cutoff, and the reports do not provide H1 FY2026 net fees or a full-year reported fee bridge; the net-fee estimate is therefore inferred from FY2025, Q4 growth rates, disposal information and cycle direction. The £37m–£46m figure is an external consensus range that management referenced, rather than formal company range guidance, although management explicitly indicated its top end. There is no direct FY2026 pre-exceptional EPS guidance, so EPS is most exposed to unobserved finance cost, tax and full-year basic-share-count outcomes. Peer evidence is indirect and has different geography/mix; German hiring, contractor hours, FX, and the final execution/timing of cost actions would change the estimates.
